title: Alpha and beta
objectives: Regress a stock on the market and interpret alpha and beta.
Judge whether an alpha is real from its standard error

screens.title: Stock against market
screens.prose: Thirty-six months. Each point is one month: the market's return above cash against a stock's return above cash, in %. The line is the least squares fit, $\hat y = 0.25 + 1.20x$.
screens.question: In a month when the market exactly matches cash, what does the line predict for the stock's excess return?

widget.label: Predicted stock excess return
widget.accept: 0.25%: the line at $x = 0$ is its intercept.

hints.text: A market excess return of 0 means $x = 0$.

feedback.correct: 0.25% a month: the part of the stock's return the market does not explain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the line at $x = 0$.

byKey.slope: 1.20 is the slope: the extra stock return per 1% of market. At $x = 0$ only the intercept is left.
byKey.zero: You assumed a stock earns nothing when the market is flat. The line says 0.25% on average.
byKey.sum: You added the slope to the intercept. That is the prediction at $x = 1$, not 0.

explain.text: At $x = 0$ the line gives its intercept, 0.25%. The slope, 1.20, is the stock's **beta**: its exposure to the market. The intercept is its **alpha**: the average return the market does not explain.

screens.title: How firmly is alpha fixed?
screens.prose: Keep the slope at 1.20 and slide the line up and down. The corner shows the sum of squared residuals. Try $\alpha = -0.6$ and $\alpha = 1.1$, each about 0.85 from the best value.

derive.caption: $\alpha$ = {{fixed(a, 2)}}% a month. Sum of squares rises {{fixed(36*pow(a - 0.25, 2), 1)}} above its least value, 850

screens.question: Moving $\alpha$ by 0.85 either way raises the sum of squares by about how much?

options.text: About 3%: the data barely prefer one alpha
It roughly doubles
options.why: Look at the corner again at $\alpha = 1.1$. The sum moves from 850 to about 875.

options.text: Not at all: alpha does not affect the fit
options.why: The sum does rise, from 850 to about 875. It is smallest at 0.25.

options.text: By a factor of ten
options.why: You may have watched the line, not the number. The corner moves by only about 25.

hints.text: About 875 against 850 is a rise of about 3%.

feedback.correct: A shift that large changes the fit by only 3%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the corner at 0.25 and at 1.1.

explain.text: With the slope fixed, the sum of squares is $850 + 36(\alpha - 0.25)^2$. A shift of 0.85, a 10% a year swing, adds only 25. Thirty-six noisy months cannot pin alpha down.

screens.title: Alpha a year
screens.prose: We regressed the stock's excess return on the market's: $$r_s - r_f = \alpha + \beta(r_m - r_f) + \epsilon.$$ In the CAPM, $\alpha = 0$: only market exposure earns a premium. Our fit gives $\hat\alpha = 0.25$% a month.
screens.question: What is $\hat\alpha$ in % a year?

hints.text: A year has twelve months of alpha.
Average returns add up over time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the monthly alpha by 12.

byKey.root: You scaled by $\sqrt{12}$. That is for volatility. An average return scales with time, so multiply by 12.
byKey.month: That is the monthly figure. A year holds twelve of them.

explain.text: Mean returns grow with time, so $12 \times 0.25 = 3.0$% a year. Compounding gives $1.0025^{12} - 1 = 3.04$%. Volatilities, by contrast, grow with $\sqrt{12}$.

screens.title: The error of alpha
screens.prose: A market-neutral fund has 36 months of residuals with standard deviation $s = 1$% a month. Its market returns average close to 0, so $\bar x^2 / S_{xx}$ is tiny and $$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) = s\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n} + \tfrac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}} \approx \frac{s}{\sqrt n}.$$
screens.question: What is the fund's $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha)$, in % a month?

byKey.by-n: You divided by 36. The error of a mean shrinks with $\sqrt n$, so divide by 6.
byKey.s: 1% is the noise in one month. The alpha averages 36 months.

explain.text: $1/\sqrt{36} = 0.167$% a month. Even with only 1% of monthly noise, an alpha of 2% a year sits just one error from zero. For our stock, with $s = 5$%, $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) = 0.84$%.

screens.title: How much is market?
screens.prose: The fit splits the stock's variation in two: the market part, $\hat\beta^2 S_{xx}$, and the rest, SSE. Here $\hat\beta = 1.20$, the market's $S_{xx} = 708.75$ and $\mathrm{SSE} = 850$.

state.caption: Residual sd $s = 5.0$% a month: the stock's own, idiosyncratic risk

screens.question: What share of the stock's variance is market, the regression's $R^2$?

feedback.correct: About 55% of the variance is market.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the market part by the total, market part plus SSE.

byKey.no-sq: You used $\hat\beta$ instead of $\hat\beta^2$. Variance scales with the square of the exposure.
byKey.flip: That is the idiosyncratic share, $850 / 1870.6$. $R^2$ is the market share.
byKey.ratio: You divided the market part by SSE alone. Divide by the total.

explain.text: The market explains $1020.6 / 1870.6 = 55$% of the stock's variance. The other 45% is idiosyncratic: $s = 5$% a month, about 17% a year. Diversification removes that part; beta cannot be diversified away.

screens.title: The market on itself
screens.prose: As a check on our code, we regress the market index's excess return on itself.
screens.question: What do we get?

options.text: $\hat\alpha = 0$, $\hat\beta = 1$, $R^2 = 1$
$\hat\alpha$ equals the market's average excess return
options.why: You expected the intercept to keep the average. The slope of 1 carries all of it, so nothing is left for $\hat\alpha$.

options.text: $\hat\beta = 1$ but $R^2$ below 1, because returns are noisy
options.why: Every point lies exactly on $y = x$, so every residual is 0 and $R^2 = 1$.

options.text: No answer: a variable cannot predict itself
options.why: It can, perfectly. The fit is $y = x$ with zero residuals.

hints.text: The line $y = 0 + 1x$ passes through every point.

feedback.correct: A perfect fit: the index has beta 1 and no alpha against itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the line through every point.

explain.text: Every point lies on $y = x$, so $\hat\alpha = 0$, $\hat\beta = 1$ and every residual is 0. This is a good test for any beta code. A fund that hugs its index looks close to this.

screens.title: Three per cent a year
screens.prose: Our stock's $\hat\alpha = 0.25$% a month is 3% a year. A broker's note calls it a stock with 3% of alpha that beats the market. Its standard error is 0.84% a month.
screens.question: What do the data say about the stock's alpha?

options.text: Nothing yet: $t = 0.30$, and the 95% interval runs from about $-1.4$ to $1.9$% a month
It beats the market by 3% a year
options.why: You read a positive alpha as an edge without its error. It is only 0.3 errors from zero.

options.text: Its alpha is 0, since the test fails
options.why: You read not significant as zero. Alphas from $-17$% to $+23$% a year all fit.

options.text: The edge comes from its beta of 1.20
options.why: Beta is market exposure, which the regression already removed. Alpha is what is left.

hints.text: Divide the alpha by its standard error.
With 34 degrees of freedom the interval is about $0.25 \pm 2.03 \times 0.84$.

feedback.correct: A $t$ of 0.3: no evidence either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the alpha next to its standard error.

byKey.skill: You called a positive alpha skill without its error. At $t = 0.30$, a stock with no alpha would look this good three times in four.
byKey.negative: You read not significant as zero. The data cannot tell 0 from 3% a year, or from $-10$%.

explain.text: $t = 0.25 / 0.84 = 0.30$ and $p = 0.77$. The 95% interval, $0.25 \pm 2.03 \times 0.84$, runs from $-1.45$ to $1.95$% a month. Reporting an alpha without its error says nothing.

screens.title: Raw or excess returns?
screens.prose: Suppose a colleague regresses raw returns, $r_s$ on $r_m$, with a constant cash rate $r_f$. Find what their intercept measures.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $r_s = \alpha + r_f - \beta r_f + \beta r_m + \epsilon$: add $r_f$ to both sides and expand the bracket
$r_s = [\alpha + (1 - \beta) r_f] + \beta r_m + \epsilon$: collect the constant terms
The raw intercept is $\alpha + (1 - \beta) r_f$, and the slope is still $\beta$: match the constant and the coefficient

hints.text: Start from the model we trust, in excess returns.
Move $r_f$ to the right and multiply out $\beta(r_m - r_f)$.
Collect everything that is not multiplied by $r_m$.

feedback.correct: The raw intercept mixes alpha with $(1 - \beta) r_f$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the excess-return model and rearrange it into raw returns.

byKey.e3: Collecting terms needs the bracket expanded first.
byKey.e4: Reading off the intercept is the last step.

explain.text: The raw intercept is $\alpha + (1 - \beta) r_f$. With cash at 0.4% a month and $\beta = 1.2$, it is $0.25 - 0.08 = 0.17$, which our data confirm. For a utility with $\beta = 0.5$ it adds 0.2% a month of fake alpha when rates are high.

screens.title: Reading the regression
screens.prose:
$$r_s - r_f = \alpha + \beta(r_m - r_f) + \epsilon$$
- $\hat\beta$: market exposure; $\hat\alpha$: the average return the market does not explain, times 12 for a year. 
- $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) \approx s/\sqrt n$, so alpha needs long records. 
- $R^2$: the share of variance that is market.
screens.question: Which number measures the stock's idiosyncratic risk?

options.text: $s$, the residual standard deviation
$\hat\beta$
options.why: Beta measures market risk, the part that moves with the index.
That is the idiosyncratic share of variance, not the risk itself in % a month.

options.text: $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\beta)$
options.why: That measures how well we know beta, not how much the stock moves on its own.

hints.text: Idiosyncratic risk is what the market does not explain.
The residuals are what the market does not explain.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the number that measures the size of the residuals.

explain.text: The residuals are the stock's own moves, so their standard deviation $s$ is its idiosyncratic risk. $1 - R^2$ gives the same thing as a share of variance. Beta measures the market part.

screens.title: A fund's claim
screens.prose: A fund claims 3% a year of alpha over three years of monthly returns. Its residuals against the market have $s = 2$% a month. Use $\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) \approx s/\sqrt n$.
screens.question: What is the $t$ statistic of the fund's alpha?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put alpha and its error in the same monthly units.

byKey.annual: You divided the annual alpha, 3%, by a monthly error. Convert to 0.25% a month first.
byKey.annual-se: You annualised the error with $\sqrt{12}$ but not with 12. Keep both monthly.

explain.text: $t = 0.25 / 0.333 = 0.75$, so $p = 0.46$. To reach $t = 2$ the fund would need $(2 \times 2 / 0.25)^2 = 256$ months: over 21 years. Most claimed alphas are untestable on short records.

screens.title: Alpha and beta in NumPy
screens.prose: Write the regression the way a risk system would. Inputs are raw monthly returns, in %, and the cash rate `rf`, one number or one per month. Fit excess on excess with the normal equations, as in least squares lesson 12.
screens.question: Complete `alpha_beta` so it returns `[alpha, beta]`, each rounded to 6 places.

widget.starter:

def alpha_beta(rs, rm, rf):
    rf = np.array(rf, dtype=float)
    y = ...   # stock excess returns
    x = ...   # market excess returns
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    a, b = ...  # solve the normal equations
    return [round(float(a), 6), round(float(b), 6)]
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def alpha_beta(rs, rm, rf):
    rf = np.array(rf, dtype=float)
    y = np.array(rs, dtype=float) - rf
    x = np.array(rm, dtype=float) - rf
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    a, b = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A, A.T @ y)
    return [round(float(a), 6), round(float(b), 6)]
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, including least squares lesson 12's data and this lesson's 36 months. Each [alpha, beta] is compared with math.isclose. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: NumPy subtracts a single number or a same-length array alike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract `rf` from both series, then solve $\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{y}$.

explain.text: Excess returns on both sides make the intercept a true alpha. Our 36 months give 0.250024 and 1.199952. The index on itself gives 0 and 1, the check from earlier.

ideas: Regress excess on excess: $\hat\beta$ is market exposure and $\hat\alpha$ the average return the market does not explain, times 12 for a year.
$\mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha) \approx s/\sqrt n$, so an alpha needs a long record: 36 months of 1% noise still leave an error of 0.17% a month.
$s$ is idiosyncratic risk and $R^2$ the share of variance that is market. Hedge with $\beta$ pounds of index per pound of stock.

formula.name: Market model
formula.note: Raw returns put $(1 - \beta) r_f$ into the intercept.

summary.trap: A positive alpha is not skill until you divide it by its standard error.

quiz.prose: You hold £100,000 of a stock with $\beta = 1.2$. You want no market exposure.
quiz.question: How much of the index should you sell short?

feedback.correct: £120,000: $\beta$ pounds of index per pound of stock.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Short $\beta$ times the stock position.

byKey.same: You matched the position pound for pound. The stock moves 1.2 times the market, so short 1.2 times as much.
byKey.inv: You divided by beta. The stock moves more than the index, so short more, not less.

explain.text: A 1% market move changes the stock by about £1,200 and the short by $-$£1,200. What remains is alpha plus idiosyncratic noise.

quiz.prose: Cash pays 0.4% a month. A utility with $\beta = 0.5$ has an excess-return alpha of 0. An analyst regresses raw returns instead.
quiz.question: What intercept will the analyst find, in % a month?

feedback.correct: 0.2% a month of fake alpha, 2.4% a year.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The raw intercept is $\alpha + (1 - \beta) r_f$.

byKey.zero: You assumed raw and excess regressions agree. With $\beta \ne 1$ the cash rate leaks into the intercept.
byKey.rf: You added all of $r_f$. Only $(1 - \beta) r_f$ leaks in.
byKey.neg: $1 - \beta = 0.5$ is positive, so the leak is upward.

explain.text: Raw intercept $= 0 + (1 - 0.5) \times 0.4 = 0.2$% a month. A low-beta stock looks like it beats the market when rates are high. Excess returns remove the illusion.

quiz.prose: A stock has $\beta = 1.2$. The market's monthly sd is 5% and the residual sd is 4%.
quiz.question: What is the regression's $R^2$?

widget.label: R-squared
widget.accept: 0.692, within 0.003: market variance $1.44 \times 25 = 36$, residual variance 16, so $36/52$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $\beta^2\sigma_m^2$ with $\beta^2\sigma_m^2 + s^2$.

byKey.sd: You added standard deviations, $6 / (6 + 4)$. Variances add; standard deviations do not.
byKey.no-sq: You used $\beta$ instead of $\beta^2$. The market variance is $1.2^2 \times 25 = 36$.

explain.text: Market variance $1.2^2 \times 5^2 = 36$, residual variance $4^2 = 16$. So $R^2 = 36 / 52 = 0.69$: about 70% of the stock's variance is market.

quiz.prose: Over 60 months a fund's alpha is 0.30% a month, 3.6% a year, with residual sd 1.5% a month.
quiz.question: Is the alpha significant at 5%?

options.text: No: $\mathrm{SE} \approx 1.5/\sqrt{60} = 0.19$, so $t = 1.55$ and $p = 0.13$
Yes, because it is positive
options.why: You read the sign as evidence. The question is how many errors it sits from zero.
You divided $s$ by $n$. The error of a mean divides by $\sqrt n$.

options.text: Yes, because 3.6% a year is a large alpha
options.why: You judged the size, not the evidence. Five years of 1.5% noise cannot confirm it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the alpha by $s/\sqrt{60}$.

explain.text: $\mathrm{SE} = 1.5/\sqrt{60} = 0.194$, so $t = 1.55$ on 58 degrees of freedom and $p = 0.13$. A real 3.6% a year alpha would often look like this, but so would luck.
